articles.body:
SpaceX investor Ross Gerber, CEO of Gerber Kawasaki, said he is “disgusted” by the recent events surrounding the slowdown of Starlink services in Ukraine, which impacted the country’s military capabilities.

“As a SpaceX shareholder I am disgusted,” Gerber said Wednesday during an appearance on CNN. “I think that these decisions were strategically horrendous and from a humanity perspective, just horrible.”

“Starlink is not reliable for national security for anybody but Trump,” he added.

Following the incident, Musk claimed in a post on social platform X that only President Trump had the ability to order the slowdown, adding that while Starlink is under Musk’s SpaceX, Starshield is owned and operated by the U.S. government.

The Wall Street Journal later reported that Musk ordered the slowdown, citing U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter, prompting calls for an investigation from several Democrats.

Gerber also told CNN on Wednesday that he is “disgusted with Elon Musk.”

“Now they have given everybody a reason not to use Starlink,” the investor continued.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the slowdown a “big mistake,” while top Trump administration officials, such as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, pointed fingers at Musk.

Hegseth told reporters Tuesday that Starlink’s slowdown had nothing to do with the White House.

“There are terms of services that ultimately need to be complied to, and that’s where Starlink has the option to make those decisions,” Hegseth said.

The slowdown came after Zelensky lashed out at Trump for waiving sanctions on Russia and making a diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Zelensky on Tuesday said he discussed with Rubio about the Starshield situation and called the conversation “constructive” in a post on X .

articles.title: After saying millions of jobs will be wiped off, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says coders are about to get busier than ever: The world has …
articles.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman believes software developers could become busier than ever despite the rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI).
articles.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman believes software developers could become busier than ever despite the rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI). Speaking on a 45-minute podcast with Matthew Berman, Altman said AI has changed how programmers work but has not reduced the need for coding. Instead, he argued, the world wants far more software than people had expected. “Coders are never going to be busier than they've been and coders are never going to have more of an impact and make more money,” Altman said, explaining why AI has not led to the decline in coding work that many had predicted.Why AI has not killed coding jobsDuring the podcast, Matthew Berman asked Sam Altman why programmers had not seen their jobs disappear as AI tools became capable of writing more code. Altman said the initial reaction to AI's coding abilities was that there would be less need for human programmers. However, he said, demand for software has turned out to be much greater than expected.“The world actually had demand for just way more software than any of us thought at the time,” Altman said.According to him, AI has changed the nature of coding work rather than eliminated the need for it. As AI tools make it easier to build software, developers can take on more projects and work on tasks that were previously difficult or too time-consuming.He also pointed out that people had been certain, just six or 12 months earlier, that AI would reduce the need for coders.Sam Altman says AI could change other professions tooDuring the podcast, Sam Altman also discussed whether the same pattern could emerge in mathematics, where AI is increasingly being used to solve complex problems. He said it was still unclear whether AI would create greater demand for mathematicians in the same way it had for software developers. However, he suggested that the nature of their work could change.“Maybe we're not going to discover new math theorems or prove them in an unaided way anymore,” Altman said.He added that mathematicians could focus more on understanding new ideas, explaining them clearly and developing proofs that people can follow. Altman said there could be other tasks that mathematicians would be able to perform better with AI, although he was unsure whether this would lead to more jobs overall.The discussion also touched on the expectation that AI would reduce the amount of work people need to do. Altman said the opposite appears to be happening so far, as people continue to find more things they want to accomplish with new technology.“I think we probably will find that there's a lot of other things that mathematicians do that we really want people to do and they can do those much better,” he said.He added that technology should ideally allow people to work less and have more time for other parts of their lives. However, he noted that people often use the time saved by technology to take on more work.“I always hope that people get to work a little bit less. I get be a little bit less busy and kind of more time for everything else in their life,” Altman said.“But man, does it sure seem like we're good at wanting more out of life and wanting more out of the world and making ourselves busier.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Inside the unlikely coalition taking on prediction markets
articles.summary: A fight over who can regulate prediction markets and whether they constitute gambling is creating strange bedfellows, as the two sides dig in for a protracted legal battle with millions of dollars at stake. The commercial gaming industry finds itself aligned with tribal gaming and unions, as they argue states and tribes should be able…
articles.body:
A fight over who can regulate prediction markets and whether they constitute gambling is creating strange bedfellows, as the two sides dig in for a protracted legal battle with millions of dollars at stake.

The commercial gaming industry finds itself aligned with tribal gaming and unions, as they argue states and tribes should be able to enforce their gambling laws against prediction markets.

It’s an unusual coalition, bringing together organizations that haven’t always seen eye to eye in the past. But they’re increasingly showing a unified front, as they face off against the platforms, which have the backing of the Trump administration.

“To see us sitting on the same side of the table advocating together is something I would have never thought would have happened,” James Siva, chairman of the California Nations Indian Gaming Association (CNIGA), said of their work alongside the unions.

The legal battle over prediction markets hinges on a relatively technical dispute — when is a wager on an event considered a financial instrument known as a “swap” instead of gambling?

States and tribes argue that prediction markets offer plain old gambling. Since gambling has historically been regulated at the state and tribal level, they contend these platforms fall under their jurisdiction and need to comply with their laws.

But prediction markets argue their products are distinct from traditional gambling and should be regulated as swaps by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), a stance the agency has also adopted and sought to aggressively enforce.

The dispute has quickly wound its way through the courts amid a deluge of lawsuits from prediction markets, states, tribes and the CFTC.

After a pair of appellate courts reached conflicting decisions, New Jersey asked the Supreme Court to take up its case against Kalshi in early September.

They received support, in the form of amicus briefs, from a bipartisan group of 39 state attorneys general, the American Gaming Association (AGA) and 145 federally recognized tribes and tribal organizations, including the Indian Gaming Association (IGA).

Commercial and tribal gaming have a somewhat contentious history. IGA Chairman David Bean acknowledged this dynamic while sharing the stage with AGA President and CEO Bill Miller at a major industry trade show in Las Vegas late last month.

“We weren’t always welcome in Las Vegas,” Bean said at the Global Gaming Expo. “But thanks to [former] Chairman [Ernie] Stevens’s perseverance and willingness to endure some somewhat hostile and unwelcoming behavior, he forged a relationship with the American Gaming Association.”

While efforts were already underway to improve this relationship, Siva underscored that prediction markets have “really been the catalyst to show that we have a lot more in common than I think we probably on both sides understood or recognized.”

“Having those two gentlemen share the stage and be aligned on this issue, I think showed how important this is,” Siva added of the AGA and IGA heads, who he joined on stage in Las Vegas. “That you have the two leaders of the two largest tribal and commercial gaming associations walking together in lockstep on this issue.”

They have found support from another unexpected contingent — labor unions. Despite previous tensions, unions are working alongside both the gaming industry and tribes to push back against platforms that they worry could threaten the jobs of their members.

UNITE HERE, which represents workers in the gaming industry, signed onto a letter in June with AGA and IGA, urging senators to explicitly prohibit event contracts tied to sports and casino-style gaming.

They were joined by several of UNITE HERE’s local units, as well as the Hotel & Gaming Trades Council, AFL-CIO, a union for hotel and gaming workers in New York and New Jersey.

“While our organizations may differ on other issues, including gambling policy, we are united in our concern that prediction markets have fueled the largest expansion of gambling in U.S. history over the past 18 months—without voter approval or legislative authorization,” they wrote.

UNITE HERE President Gwen Mills also made an appearance at the Global Gaming Expo last month, joining Miller on a panel about confronting prediction markets, where he welcomed her as the “most recent addition to this formidable coalition.”

Chris Cylke, AGA’s senior vice president of government relations, said it “wasn’t a hard sell” to get unions on board on this issue.

“Because of the fact that we are, whether it’s tribal gaming or commercial gaming, large employers in a lot of communities across the country … and a high percentage of the jobs we have are unionized, it wasn’t a hard sell to our friends at the unions to impress upon them that they were also potentially at risk,” Cylke told The Hill.

Aamir Deen, an organizer with UNITE HERE, underscored there isn’t as much overlap between the groups in other situations. But he added, “when it comes to prediction markets, there’s a great deal of common ground between us and the entire industry.”

The unions and tribes have their own complicated history, particularly in California.

“There’s been instances where we feel like the unions are either ignoring our sovereignty or treading on our sovereignty,” Siva said.

Deen, who works with UNITE HERE’s Local 49 in the Sacramento area, also noted that “the history of my union and tribes in California is long and deep and has been very contentious in the past.”

He acknowledged that the union’s efforts at bargaining and organizing have sometimes put them at odds with the tribes but suggested this has also allowed them to build a relationship that “opened the door to talking about some of these other issues.”

“While the relationship remains complicated on this issue, we have found ourselves sitting on the same side of the table,” Siva added.

“That’s been a very powerful message to deliver, especially to the California leadership out in D.C. on the Hill, the members of Congress from California who understand the very kind of diverse and often negative history that we’ve had with those groups,” he continued.

Cylke similarly suggested the diverse nature of this coalition is working to its advantage in Washington.

“Having a united front, where all the groups are in these meetings together and can say, ‘You know, look, we don’t agree on everything, but we agree wholeheartedly that what prediction markets are doing is wrong’ … It’s a really powerful message.”

articles.body:
Two Air Force pilots safely ejected from their aircraft near San Antonio on Thursday because of potential issues with their landing gear.

The pilots — who were part of a training program at Joint Base San Antonio-Randolph in Texas — received indications their landing gear was unsafe and ejected at the recommendation of experts, a statement from the base said. The pilots were evaluated by local medical personnel.

“Two pilots successfully ejected from a T-6A Texan II assigned to the 12th Flying Training Wing during a controlled bailout near Seguin, Texas,” a release from the base states.

The 12th Flying Training Wing is a program that develops enlisted Air Force aviators and crew members through “flying training and education.” Airmen in the program are trained in a variety of disciplines including combat systems officer training, pilot instructor training and enlisted aviator training.

The sheriff’s office for nearby Wilson County said in a Thursday Facebook post that they were responding to the scene of an “aircraft accident” along with a number of other agencies. They affirmed that there was no threat to the public.

“You can expect a large presence of law enforcement, military, fire, and EMS personnel,” the Wilson County Sheriff’s Office wrote at the time.

articles.title: Lab testing giant Quest Diagnostics confirms patients' personal and health data was compromised during breach | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Quest is the latest in a series of healthcare technology companies that have been hacked in recent months.
articles.body:
Medical lab testing giant Quest Diagnostics has confirmed a cyberattack and data breach affecting an as-yet unspecified amount of sensitive patient information stored in its systems, according to a legally required disclosure with U.S. regulators.

Quest said in an 8-K filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission that it learned of a cyberattack on Wednesday targeting one of its lab testing systems, Quanum, which allows doctors’ offices, hospitals, and healthcare practices to request lab tests for patients while also handling billing. The platform stores a large amount of patient health and medical records, as well as associated diagnostic and billing data.

The company said the unauthorized access included the accessing of “certain patient records.” Quest said it notified law enforcement and is investigating.

The cyberattack on Quest is the latest major cyber incident to affect the healthcare industry this year. A series of cyberattacks and data breaches have sparked weeks of disruption and allowed the theft of millions of patient electronic health records and other medical information. Health tech companies have become a major target for financially motivated cybercriminals, who aim to steal as much sensitive data as possible and threaten to publish it if they aren’t paid a ransom.

In recent months, a cyberattack resulted in the mass-wiping of employee devices at medical tech maker Stryker in March, and a hack on medical implant manufacturer Boston Scientific in August forced the company’s network offline for weeks, sparking “global disruption” to its operations. Meanwhile, separate hacks throughout the year caused massive breaches of patient data at medical recordkeeping company CareCloud , Scotland-based health tech provider Craneware , and U.S. pharmaceutical distribution giant McKesson .

The lab-testing giant has not yet said how many healthcare customers, or patients, had information stolen during the attack on its Quanum systems.

Quest’s website and materials say Quanum is used by about half a million clinicians in thousands of locations across North America. It’s unclear how many health records Quanum holds, but one 2026 case study on Quest’s website shows how a single health system with more than 6 million patients can hold hundreds of millions of related medical documents and charts.

Quest did not say when the breach began or whether any hacking group has contacted the company with demands, such as payment in exchange to not release the stolen data. Amanda Rivera, a spokesperson for Quest, did not answer TechCrunch’s questions about the incident and referred to its security notice .

In the notice , Quest said that some patients’ protected health information was taken, including “personal information and patient records,” but the company is still investigating what specific kinds of data were taken. (The website post currently contains “noindex” code , which tells search engines not to list the page in search results, making it far more difficult for people to find the page.)

This is Quest’s second known major data breach in a decade, after losing 11.9 million patient records in a cyberattack on a third-party billing company in 2019.

Do you work at Quest Diagnostics or know more about the data breach? We’d love to hear from you. You can reach this reporter on Signal at the username zackwhittaker.1337 or by email [email protected] .

articles.title: Feds want robotaxis to signal ‘I’m driving’ with cyan-colored lights
articles.summary: NHTSA proposes updating federal safety rules to allow cyan lights for autonomous vehicles and remove legacy human-driver requirements like turn signal levers.
articles.body: After years of debating how driverless cars should tell the world no one is at the wheel — flashing text, audio alerts, custom lights — the feds just stepped in with a single answer: cyan. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration released proposed changes to Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard (FMVSS) No. 108, specifically rewriting the rules to fit autonomous vehicles. It’s a mix of cutting red tape for human-free designs and standardizing how robotaxis communicate with the world around them — starting with a distinctive blue-green light. NHTSA is proposing cyan-colored marker lamps “to clearly and consistently signal to law enforcement and other road users when an automated driving system is operating the vehicle.” Why cyan? The auto industry already uses red, amber, white, and flashing blue/red lights for such things as brakes, turn signals, headlights, and emergency vehicles. Cyan could theoretically fill the visual gap without confusing road users. And there’s some precedent, too. Mercedes-Benz got state-level approval for turquoise lights on its Level 3 Drive Pilot cars — even though the automaker has since scrapped the idea in favor of a Level 2++ system. Nevertheless, NHTSA wants to set a national standard that robotaxi operators like Waymo, Nuro, and Zoox, as well as automakers like GM and Mercedes, can adopt uniformly. Under the proposed rule, cyan marker lights would be optional for manufacturers. However, by creating official federal standards for their color, brightness, and location, NHTSA wants to make sure that any automaker who chooses to add them uses a consistent, legal setup instead of a confusing mix of different colors and signals. NHTSA is also proposing to get rid of some lighting requirements that wouldn’t make sense for a vehicle without a human driver. Current rules demand physical hazard switches, manual beam shifters, and turn levers inside the vehicles. The agency is proposing to remove these requirements, while also updating the 12.8-volt testing standard so automakers can build around modern LED architectures without jumping through administrative hoops. And NHTSA is considering getting rid of requirements dictating whether high-beam lights sit above or below low-beam lights. This update is part of the broader administrative push by the Department of Transportation to streamline AV deployment. The government wants to make it easier for automakers to build cars without traditional controls, like steering wheel and pedals, that are meant for vehicles that are operated by human drivers. That said, regulators are also still enforcing the rules as they’re written. Last month, NHTSA opened an audit query into the Tesla Cybercab “to examine the process and technical data on which Tesla relied when certifying the Cybercab and related issues.” At issue is the absence of certain design features such as sideview mirrors, pedals, and steering wheel — all of which are required under FMVSS.

articles.title: New Florida counties report dengue cases as statewide total passes 400
articles.summary: Pinellas County is continuing to see a spike in dengue fever cases as the state’s dengue fever outbreak shows no sign of slowing.
articles.body:
TAMPA, Fla. ( WFLA ) – Florida’s Pinellas County is continuing to see a spike in dengue fever cases as the state’s outbreak shows no sign of slowing.

Across the state of Florida, 425 locally acquired dengue fevers have been reported since the year began, with the majority of cases being reported in Hillsborough County.

Florida’s outbreak was largely concentrated in Hillsborough County until recent weeks, when Pinellas County has been seeing spikes in local cases as well.

The table below lists which counties have reported cases as of last week.

In addition to the 425 locally acquired cases, there were 288 international cases reported in Florida as well.

USF professor Benjamin Jacob and his team are using AI to target breeding grounds for mosquitoes carrying the dengue virus.

“This system that we’re using, which I call Seek and Destroy, is a system that I actually originated in Africa where I was fighting malaria for the last ten years, and we’re still continuing,” explained Jacob.

The system uses satellite infrared images combined with weather patterns and known breeding grounds to spot even more potential locations in a matter of minutes.

“I can find it remotely. I can use satellite data systems with AI to find the habitats that you can’t find. Because I’m looking at it from an overhead point of view,” said Jacob.

The USF group then gives that information to the state who can treat the problem.

Hillsborough county mosquito control is also collaborating with USF. The county continues to be the hotspot for not only the Tampa Bay area, but the state. There is, however, some promise: 36 reported cases within the past week are down from the 79 cases reported the week before.

“That shows a nice slow,” said Gabriel Henderson with Hillsborough County Mosquito Control. “Hopefully, with this cooler weather, that will also create the right kind of environment for us to be able to continue and make sure we are knocking down those numbers even further.”

Hillsborough County Mosquito Control says the main concern for spread still remains in central Tampa, but now cases are starting move east toward Brandon.

“Not necessarily like more numbers, but just some cases in that area that weren’t there before,” explained Henderson.

articles.body:
Hurricane Vance is expected to steadily intensify in the next 24 hours and turn into a major hurricane by Friday night, according to projections from the National Hurricane Center.

“Swells generated by Vance are expected to begin affecting portions of the coast of southern and southwestern Mexico this weekend and continue into next week,” the hurricane center said in an advisory Friday morning .

“These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions,” the advisory said.

Vance, which became a hurricane Friday, was a Category 1 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 90 mph and could become a major Category 3 hurricane before the end of Friday, The Associated Press reported.

It could be the seventh major hurricane in a row this year in the Pacific Ocean, following Nolo, Odalys, Polo, Rachel, Simon and Trudy.

The northeastern and central Pacific basins saw a number of powerful storms this year, with at least 20 named storms in the region by Sept. 28, according to a NASA report . Nine of those storms reached hurricane strength.

The intense hurricane season in the Pacific comes as El Niño conditions create unusual weather patterns.

In July, the AP reported that this year’s El Niño had an 81 percent chance of becoming “very strong” by fall, altering weather patterns across the globe.

articles.title: Nationwide recall on these compound GLP-1 drugs
articles.summary: The compounded GLP-1s are not FDA-approved nor name-brand.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — The FDA has issued a recall for 23 GLP-1 compounded vials from Apothecary Pharma LLC due to lack of assurance the vials are sterile.

The FDA has designated the recall as Class II , meaning exposure to the products could cause reversible or temporary health consequences and poses little risk of serious consequences from use, according to the FDA website.

The recall applies to 22 vials of Tirzepatide Injection, 18mg/mL, 4 mL Sterile Multi-Dose Vial, Rx only, Apothecary Pharma, LLC, 1913 Evans Road, Cary, NC 27513, NDC 85091-001-18. Tirzepatide is used in Zepbound and Mounjaro. Customers should look out for these specific codes:

The recall also applies to one vial of NAD+ Injection 200 mg/mL, 6 mL Sterile Multi-Dose Vial, Rx Only, Apothecary Pharma, LLC, 1913 Evans Road, Cary, NC, 27513, NDC 85091-011-06. The code information is: Lot #: AP-202647, BUD 13-Oct-2026

Compounding pharmacy flagged by the FDA before

Apothecary Pharma in December 2025 received a letter from the FDA stating, “FDA investigators noted that drug products intended or expected to be sterile were prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions, whereby they may have become contaminated with filth or rendered injurious to health, causing your drug products to be adulterated under section 501(a)(2)(A) of the FDCA.”

Apothecary Pharma LLC is a compounding pharmacy in North Carolina. Compounded GLP-1s are not FDA-approved or name-brand. These pharmacies create customized versions of drugs for patients rather than mass-producing them like a commercial pharmacy, and they can adjust medications and create new versions to meet the patient’s specific needs

Although these pharmacies use FDA-approved ingredients, the products themselves are not checked for effectiveness, safety or purity, according to an article in Harvard Health Publishing. The FDA occasionally grants these pharmacies permission to produce drugs in bulk during shortages. In 2022, compounders were given permission to produce their own GLP-1 drugs to fill a shortage at the time. However, tirzepatide and semaglutide were removed from the drug shortage list in late 2024 and early 2025, according to Pharmacy Times reporting. Compound pharmacies continue to produce GLP-1s despite the lack of a shortage.

The FDA has not released official instructions on what to do if you discover you purchased a recalled vial; no illnesses have been linked to the recall at this time. Consumers should stop using it and contact their healthcare provider for guidance.

articles.body:
President Trump says the NFL should have considered postponing a game set to be played in France on Sunday between the New Orleans Saints and Pittsburgh Steelers amid social unrest in the country.

Trump told reporters on Friday he was “worried” about the game, saying “it’s looking like tomorrow is going to be a bad day in France, so you worry about it.”

“I would’ve said the NFL could’ve probably postponed that match,” he continued. “France is really in trouble. That’s what happens when you go left.”

The president’s comments appear to contradict Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who a day earlier said, “our embassy feels the game will be fine,” when asked about the Steelers vs. Saints clash.

The game, slated for 9:30 a.m. EDT at Stade de France near Paris, is one of nearly a dozen the NFL is playing internationally this season.

France has been rocked in recent days by protests that have escalated into rioting, as citizens voice displeasure with education and other issues relating to the government.

Trump and the GOP have pointed to the rioting as a warning for Americans about embracing what they say are progressive policies.

The NFL has not announced any change in plans relative to Sunday’s game.

articles.title: Trump says wind turbine part imports cause national security issue, but doesn’t impose tariffs
articles.summary: The Trump administration has determined that imports of wind turbine parts pose a national security threat, but it does not appear to be opting to tariff them. President Trump issued a memo Thursday saying “wind turbines and their components and subcomponents are being imported into the United States under such circumstances as to threaten to…
articles.body:
The Trump administration has determined that imports of wind turbine parts pose a national security threat, but it does not appear to be opting to tariff them.

President Trump issued a memo Thursday saying “wind turbines and their components and subcomponents are being imported into the United States under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States.”

But the memo stopped short of saying there should be tariffs on imported wind turbines. Instead, it said the U.S. should negotiate with trading partners to “adjust” imports of wind turbines and their components.

Trump has been a longtime critic of wind energy and has particularly decried turbines as ugly. His administration has put up a number of hurdles for the buildout of renewable energy broadly and wind in particular, including claims that they could interfere with national security and radars.

Wind supporters have criticized such claims as a pretext to block an energy source the president simply does not like.

Trump’s latest memo says that wind turbines containing foreign-made parts may “contain cybersecurity vulnerabilities that could lead to remote control access to wind turbines and cause power disruption.”

It also criticized wind more broadly as an “unreliable and intermittent energy source.”

articles.title: Ukraine: Starlink still isn’t working after Trump restoration promise
articles.summary: Ukraine’s military on Friday struggled with a still-slowed Starlink satellite system despite President Trump’s promise a day earlier that SpaceX owner Elon Musk had restored the service. Connections with Starshield — the military version of Starlink, a major tool for Ukraine to defend itself from missile and drone attacks from Russia — continued to fail…
articles.body:
Ukraine’s military on Friday struggled with a still-slowed Starlink satellite system despite President Trump’s promise a day earlier that SpaceX owner Elon Musk had restored the service.

Connections with Starshield — the military version of Starlink, a major tool for Ukraine to defend itself from missile and drone attacks from Russia — continued to fail in most of the country if drones flew faster than 100 mph, The Wall Street Journal reported .

“The speed limits on Starlink and Starshield are still there, and the speed has not been restored,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in remarks on Friday.

He said Ukraine hopes SpaceX and the Trump administration will fully restore the service: “We count on such decisions.”

The Journal reported Thursday that Trump called Musk on Wednesday to ask that he remove restrictions on Starshield. The outlet earlier in the week reported that Musk ordered the slowdown of the satellite services.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, Trump denied speaking to Musk about the tech leader’s decision to restrict Starlink for Ukraine but said he will do so if access is not restored.

“I have not spoken to him,” Trump told reporters on the White House South Lawn. “I might have to, but I have not. I have heard it was fixed. If it’s not, I’ll speak to him.”

Asked who had initially ordered the slowdown, Trump said, “I have no idea, but I wouldn’t tell you if I did.”

Ukraine’s military has been kneecapped since Oct. 14 after Starlink and Starshield connections in the country were slowed without warning. The system’s degradation came after Zelensky lashed out at Trump for waiving sanctions on Russia and making a deal to purchase diesel from Russian President Vladimir Putin. Zelensky called Trump “weak” for making the deal.

The Starlink restrictions have disrupted any military equipment that moves at high speeds, making it difficult for Ukraine to use interceptor drones to defend against Russian attacks.

Musk last week denied being behind the issue, instead placing blame on the Trump administration.

“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he said in a social media post.

articles.title: Paxton sues OpenAI, Altman for failing to warn Texans about ChatGPT’s ‘dangers’
articles.summary: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) sued OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman on Friday, accusing the company of failing to warn consumers about the potential dangers from its AI models. The lawsuit alleges the ChatGPT maker is running afoul of a Texas consumer protection law and kids’ online safety law, underscoring warnings about the…
articles.body:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) sued OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman on Friday, accusing the company of failing to warn consumers about the potential dangers from its AI models.

The lawsuit alleges the ChatGPT maker is running afoul of a Texas consumer protection law and kids’ online safety law, underscoring warnings about the technology’s risks from AI leaders, including Altman .

“Despite these incredible dangers, Altman and OpenAI have not only barreled ahead in creating these risks but have done so by unlawfully deceiving Texans about the safety, accuracy, and reliability of their products,” the complaint reads.

“Defendants have built an artificial intelligence empire on the backs of Texans by deceiving them, while at the same time endangering public health,” it continues.

While its products are marketed as “trustworthy, reliable, and safe,” Paxton argues ChatGPT is prone to errors and hallucinations, in which AI tools produce fake results.

He suggests this “unreliability is dangerous,” pointing to users who have relied on incorrect or misleading healthcare information from ChatGPT.

The Texas attorney general also alleges OpenAI has failed to put in place proper safeguards for minors as required under the state’s Securing Children Online Through Parental Empowerment Act.

Paxton further argues the company cannot control its technology, highlighting a series of recent incidents in which AI agents hacked into other organizations or acted in unexpected ways.

“As part of our focus on responsibly delivering the benefits of AI, we’ve worked closely with experts to continually improve ChatGPT, mitigate risks and build additional safeguards,” an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement to The Hill.

“Governments have an important role to play in setting robust safety standards for AI, and we’re committed to working with Texas and other states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry – not just one company.”

Eight other states — Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho, Montana, Iowa, Kansas, West Virginia and Nebraska — sued the ChatGPT maker earlier this month, similarly arguing the company misled users about the safety of its chatbot.

Florida separately sued OpenAI in June, alleging it promoted a product it knew could harm consumers.

“With the rapid advancement of AI technology, OpenAI has the responsibility to protect users and warn them of the many dangers of its platform,” Paxton said in a statement Friday. “I will fight to protect Texans from the harms of AI and ensure that powerful technology companies are not above the law.”

Paxton is currently facing off against Democrat James Talarico in a tight race for the Lone Star state’s Senate seat.

Despite President Trump’s forceful embrace of AI, Paxton and several other GOP candidates have sought some distance on issues surrounding the technology, most notably data centers.

The Texas attorney general unveiled a plan in August to place restrictions on the controversial AI infrastructure if he is elected to the Senate.

articles.title: West Virginia attorney general subpoenas environmental groups
articles.summary: West Virginia’s attorney general has sent investigative subpoenas to environmental advocacy organizations — something the groups are describing as a retaliatory attack on their First Amendment rights. West Virginia Rivers Coalition and 350.org filed a lawsuit this week saying they and at least four other organizations received subpoenas from the office of state Attorney General…
articles.body:
West Virginia’s attorney general has sent investigative subpoenas to environmental advocacy organizations — something the groups are describing as a retaliatory attack on their First Amendment rights.

West Virginia Rivers Coalition and 350.org filed a lawsuit this week saying they and at least four other organizations received subpoenas from the office of state Attorney General JB McCuskey (R).

The demands seek information about the organizations’ public statements about climate change and energy, requests for donations, ties to renewable energy companies and more.

They asked a federal court in West Virginia to halt enforcement of the subpoenas, saying they violate the organizations’ rights to free speech and calling them “baseless and retaliatory.”

“We’ve done nothing wrong and we don’t sell anything, yet these subpoenas were issued under a law meant to protect consumers from unfair business practices. They serve no legitimate investigative purpose. They read as an attempt to pressure and intimidate people working for the public good, and we’re asking the court to stop them,” said 350.org’s executive director Anne Jellema in a written statement.

Meanwhile, at least one other group, the Sierra Club, said it received a subpoena that was later withdrawn — after it informed the attorney general’s office of its intent to sue over it.

“While we are glad to see the West Virginia attorney general withdraw his sweeping subpoena after we informed him of our plans to file a federal lawsuit, his threats to silence and intimidate us and other groups remain,” said Loren Blackford, executive director of the Sierra Club.

Blackford said the probe was unprecedented.

“We’ve seen nothing like this,” she said.

The Hill has reached out to McCuskey’s office for comment.

In the past, congressional Republicans have subpoenaed and otherwise sought to investigate environmental groups . Earlier this year, Florida’s attorney general also subpoenaed environmental law-related organizations.

Pressure increases on Trump administration over Starlink slowdown

Pressure is increasing on the Trump administration to restore and expand Ukraine’s access to Starshield satellite systems, as well as get to the bottom of who ordered the service slowed in the first place.

In a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a bipartisan group of House and Senate lawmakers – all of them staunch Ukraine allies – urged the administration not only to lift any speed restrictions related to the systems, but also to expand the Starshield contract to bolster Ukraine’s military capacity, even over Russian territory.

“Ukrainian forces depend on these services for command and control, intelligence sharing, battlefield communications, and the operation of unmanned systems,” the lawmakers wrote. “Any degradation in service, including reduced connection speeds, restricted geographic coverage, or interruptions in access, undermines Ukraine’s military effectiveness and provides Russian forces with an operational advantage that will extend the conflict and put more civilians in harm’s way.”

The letter was signed by three senators — Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) and Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) — and five members of the House: Reps. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.), Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio), Mike Quigley (D-Ill.), Jim Costa (D-Calif.) and Jimmy Panetta (D-Calif.).

The push is just the latest part of a broader outcry on Capitol Hill over reports that Starshield’s receivers quit working earlier this month for Ukrainian military equipment operating above a certain speed. Starshield is a specialized branch of the Starlink satellite systems run by SpaceX, which is owned by tech mogul Elon Musk.

Separately, three House Democrats representing Silicon Valley – Reps. Sam Liccardo, Jimmy Panetta and Ro Khanna – sent a letter to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, demanding the administration launch an investigation into the Starlink slowdown.

The three press for a briefing within two weeks outlining who was behind the decision to curtail Starshield speeds and how that was carried out.

Musk has said any decisions to restrict Starshield were not his and must have come from President Trump and the Pentagon. A recent report by The Wall Street Journal , however, contradicted that account, saying Musk was behind the restrictions. The report infuriated many lawmakers in the Capitol, who say decisions affecting the military capability of Ukraine — or any U.S. ally — should not be left in the hands of any single company.
